summary.text: Osmosis is the spontaneous net movement of solvent molecules through a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with the higher solute concentration.
In biological systems the solvent is typically water, and osmosis is the primary means by which water is transported into and out of cells.
A cell in saltwater loses water while a cell in freshwater gains it, which is why osmosis matters for keeping cells hydrated.

facts.label: Osmotic pressure
facts.value: External pressure needed to stop net solvent movement

facts.label: Role in plants
facts.value: Main agent of support in many plants

facts.value: Slices in strong salt solution shrink and lose turgor pressure

items.prompt: An animal cell is dropped into a very salty bath. Which way does water move?

options.label: Into the cell, because salt attracts water inward
Out of the cell
Neither way, since cells block all water
Into the cell until the bath is fresh

items.explain: When a cell is submerged in saltwater, water molecules move out of the cell.

items.prompt: Two identical potato slices go into salt solutions, one stronger than the other. What would you expect?

options.label: The slice in the stronger solution loses more size and weight
Both slices shrink by exactly the same amount
The slice in the weaker solution loses more size and weight
The slice in the stronger solution swells

items.explain: The more concentrated the salt solution, the bigger the loss in size and weight of the potato slice.

items.prompt: Water keeps entering a plant cell by osmosis, yet the cell does not burst. What stops it?

options.label: The membrane stops being semipermeable once full
The water leaves again as soon as it arrives
Pressure against the cell wall rises until it equals the osmotic pressure
The salt inside the cell is used up

items.explain: Osmotic entry of water raises the turgor pressure against the cell wall until it equals the osmotic pressure, creating a steady state.

items.prompt: A membrane has pure water on both sides. Are water molecules moving through it?

options.label: No, nothing moves without a concentration difference
Yes, but only toward the side with more pressure
Yes, and a net flow builds toward one side
Yes, equally in both directions, so there is no net flow

items.explain: With pure water on both sides, molecules pass in each direction at exactly the same rate, so there is no net flow.

items.prompt: Two solutions have the same molar concentration of different solutes. How do their osmotic pressures compare?

options.label: They are the same, since it depends on concentration, not on the solute's identity
The larger solute molecules give a much higher pressure
The more water-loving solute gives a higher pressure
The solution with the heavier solute gives a lower pressure

items.explain: Osmotic pressure is a colligative property: it depends on the molar concentration of the solute but not on its identity.

items.prompt: Water molecules cross a plasma membrane's phospholipid bilayer through what?

options.label: Ion pumps
Cholesterol channels
Aquaporins
Peripheral enzymes

items.explain: Water molecules travel across the phospholipid bilayer via aquaporins through a selective pore flow mechanism.

paragraphs.heading: What osmosis is
paragraphs.text: Osmosis is the drift of a solvent through a barrier that lets the solvent pass but holds back the substances dissolved in it. Such a barrier is called selectively permeable. The net flow runs from the side with less dissolved material toward the side with more, and it tends to even out the concentrations on the two sides. In living things the solvent is usually water, but the same effect can happen in other liquids and even in gases.

paragraphs.heading: Why cells depend on it
paragraphs.text: Cell membranes are barriers of this kind, so osmosis is vital in biology. They generally block ions, proteins and other large or polar molecules, while letting through fatty substances and small molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide. Osmosis is the main way water gets into and out of cells. Water crosses the membrane through pores called aquaporins.

paragraphs.heading: Which way the water goes
paragraphs.text: Put a cell in water and water crosses its membrane from the side with less solute to the side with more. A cell sitting in salt water loses water. A cell sitting in fresh water takes water in. When there is pure water on both sides of a membrane, molecules still cross in both directions, but at equal rates, so there is no net flow.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure that holds plants up
paragraphs.text: Osmotic pressure is the outside pressure you would need to apply to stop the net flow of solvent. In many plants this pressure is the main source of support. Water flowing into a plant cell raises the pressure the cell presses against its wall, called turgor pressure, until it equals the osmotic pressure and things settle. In a solution more concentrated than its cytoplasm, a plant cell loses water, shrinks and goes flaccid. In extreme cases the membrane comes away from the wall, a state called plasmolysis, while in a less concentrated solution the cell takes in water and swells until it is turgid.

paragraphs.heading: A kitchen demonstration
paragraphs.text: Potato slices dropped into strong salt water show osmosis at work. Water leaves the potato for the salty liquid, so the slices shrink and lose their turgor pressure. The saltier the solution, the more size and weight the slices lose.

paragraphs.heading: More than diffusion
paragraphs.text: Osmotic pressure depends on how much solute is dissolved, not on what that solute is; this is called a colligative property. Two proposed explanations of osmosis have both been firmly disproved. Osmosis does not depend on how big the solute molecules are or how strongly they attract water, which rules out the bound water model. Osmosis can also push water toward the side where water is more concentrated, which rules out the diffusion model. Heat from the surroundings can even be turned into mechanical energy, as water rises. So the flow of solvent is driven by pressure rather than by random wandering of molecules.

paragraphs.heading: An old observation
paragraphs.text: People have seen some kinds of osmotic flow since ancient times, for instance in the building of the Egyptian pyramids. Jean-Antoine Nollet was the first to document it, in 1748. The name grew out of endosmose and exosmose, words the French physician René Dutrochet built from Greek roots meaning within, outer and push.
